raw_case_text: A 64-year-old woman weighing 67 kg who had undergone breast cancer surgery over 10 years earlier presented with mental abnormalities 3 months before coming to the hospital for sudden-onset limb weakness. On January 14, 2021, the patient was admitted to Huizhou Third People's Hospital due to sudden weakness in her left arm and leg that lasted for 3 h. Physical examination revealed drowsiness, rightward gaze, aphasia, left facial palsy, and left-sided hemiplegia. Her initial National Institute of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score was 13. Head and neck computed tomography(CT) angiography did not show any signs of cerebral hemorrhage or large vessel occlusion (Figure 1I). Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with acute IS of undetermined cause and received intravenous thrombolysis with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rt-PA) 40 mg (0.6 mg/kg) in the emergency room. Following thrombolysis, there was improvement in the patient's neurological function such that her NIHSS score improved to 8. Brain magnetic resonance imaging(MRI) performed 24 h after thrombolysis showed infarction only in the right temporal lobe and posterior horn of the ventricle (Figure 1II). However, the patient developed a high fever 10 h after being transferred to the stroke unit. The patient's mental function also deteriorated significantly. Lumbar puncture results showed elevated total protein levels (374 mg/dL) and a high nucleated cell count (2.58 x 106/L), along with a decreased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)/blood glucose ratio. This led us to suspect that the patient had developed IS complicated by an intracranial infection. To treat the infection, we immediately administered ceftriaxone(2 g, q12h), while continuing clopidogrel (CYP2C19 genotype *1/*1) and atorvastatin for secondary prevention. However, even after three days of ceftriaxone treatment, the patient's fever persisted and the cause of the infection remained unknown. Consequently, on the third day after admission, we discontinued ceftriaxone and transitioned to meropenem (2g q8h) for continued anti-infective therapy. On the 7th day after admission, metagenome next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of CSF and venous blood cultures confirmed infection with Brucella melitensis. The new treatment plan comprised intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g, q12h), oral doxycycline (100 mg, bid), and oral rifampicin (0.6 g, qd). Notably, brain MRI conducted on the 20th day after admission revealed a new IS (Figure 1III). Subsequently, the patient's condition worsened. Her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 11 as of 44 days after admission. A brain CT scan indicated a HS of approximately 66 mL, which required an urgent craniotomy (Figure 1IV). Immunohistochemical analysis of the hematoma sample collected during the operation revealed CD4+ and C8+ T lymphocytes surrounding the blood vessels (Figure 2). Upon discharge, the patient was prescribed a 3-month regimen of atorvastatin, rifampicin, and doxycycline. The patient attended follow-up appointments at our hospital's outpatient clinic on the 7th day and 1 month after being discharged. During both visits, normal liver and kidney functions were observed. The blood routine results showed a slightly higher proportion of lymphocytes and monocytes, along with a slightly lower proportion of neutrophils and neutrophil count. Subsequent follow-up calls will occur every 3 months or semi-annually until the end of the follow-up period in February 2023. The patient had regained the ability to walk and had a modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score of 2, although she still experienced incoherent speech (Figure 3).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 64-year-old female presented with sudden weakness in her left arm and leg lasting for 3 hours, preceded by mental abnormalities for 3 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 64-year-old woman presented with acute left hemiparesis for 3 hours, preceded by a 3-month history of behavioral/mental changes. In the emergency department, she was diagnosed with acute ischemic stroke of undetermined etiology and received intravenous thrombolysis with rt-PA 40 mg (0.6 mg/kg), which improved her NIHSS score from 13 to 8. Ten hours after transfer to the stroke unit, she developed high fever and severe cognitive deterioration. Secondary stroke prevention with clopidogrel and atorvastatin was maintained, while empiric IV ceftriaxone (2 g, q12h) was initiated, escalated to IV meropenem (2 g q8h) on day 3 due to persistent fever. On day 20, she suffered a recurrent ischemic stroke. On day 44, neurological decline (GCS 11) prompted imaging that revealed a 66-mL intracerebral hemorrhage requiring emergency craniotomy.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of surgical resection for breast cancer over 10 years earlier. Mental abnormalities present for 3 months prior to presentation. Epidemiological exposure to livestock or unpasteurized dairy not documented. Home medications and allergies not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Preceding 3-month history of mental/behavioral changes; acute left hemiparesis, drowsiness, aphasia, high fever, and incoherent speech. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Body weight: 67 kg. Neurological: drowsy, rightward gaze, aphasia, left facial palsy, and left-sided hemiplegia. Initial NIHSS score: 13 (improved to 8 post-thrombolysis). Subsequent course marked by high fever, severe mental function deterioration, and Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score declining to 11 on day 44.
objective.routine_investigations: Pharmacogenomics: CYP2C19 genotype *1/*1. Follow-up laboratory evaluation: normal liver and kidney functions; blood routine showed slightly higher proportion of lymphocytes and monocytes, along with slightly lower proportion of neutrophils and neutrophil count.
objective.advanced_workup: Head and neck CT angiography: no signs of cerebral hemorrhage or large vessel occlusion. Brain MRI (24 h post-thrombolysis): infarction in right temporal lobe and posterior horn of the ventricle. Brain MRI (day 20): new acute ischemic stroke. Brain CT (day 44): hemorrhagic stroke / intracerebral hematoma of approximately 66 mL. Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis: total protein 374 mg/dL, nucleated cell count 2.58 x 106/L, and decreased CSF/blood glucose ratio. Histopathology and immunohistochemistry of evacuated hematoma: CD4+ and CD8+ T lymphocytes surrounding cerebral blood vessels, consistent with cerebral vasculitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Neurobrucellosis (Brucella melitensis CNS infection / cerebral vasculitis) complicated by recurrent ischemic strokes and catastrophic intracerebral hemorrhage requiring surgical evacuation.
Confirmation: Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of CSF and venous blood cultures confirming Brucella melitensis on day 7 post-admission.
Differentials ruled out: Large vessel atherothrombotic stroke (CTA negative for large vessel occlusion), cardiogenic embolism, routine pyogenic bacterial meningitis (fever refractory to ceftriaxone and meropenem).
Treatment & Outcome: Received acute rt-PA thrombolysis, followed by clopidogrel and atorvastatin. Following mNGS confirmation of Brucella melitensis, targeted antimicrobial therapy was initiated with intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g, q12h), oral doxycycline (100 mg, bid), and oral rifampicin (0.6 g, qd). Following secondary hemorrhagic transformation (~66 mL hematoma) on day 44, she underwent emergency craniotomy and hematoma evacuation. Discharged on a 3-month oral regimen of atorvastatin, rifampicin, and doxycycline. At long-term follow-up through February 2023, she regained unassisted ambulation with a modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score of 2, with residual incoherent speech.
